2. Even one improving circuit can contain the whole feasibility problem

The following exact reduction explains why supplying a compact feasible region and a known starting vertex does not supply the missing progress selector.

For arbitrary $A,b$, construct

$$P(A,b)=
\left\{
(u,t,w)\ge0:
Au-bt=0,\quad
\mathbf1^\top u+t+w=1
\right\}.$$

This is a nonempty compact polytope, and

$$v_0=(0,0,1)$$

is an explicitly known vertex. Give it objective $-t$.

Then

$$\boxed{
Ax=b,\ x\ge0\ \text{is feasible}
\iff
\text{there is a feasible strictly improving circuit at }v_0.
}$$

Extraction is immediate. Any such circuit $q$ must satisfy

$$q_u\ge0,\qquad q_t>0,\qquad Aq_u=bq_t.$$

Consequently,

$$x=q_u/q_t$$

is a feasible solution of the original instance.

Conversely, a feasible $x$ gives

$$p=\frac{(x,1,0)}{1+\mathbf1^\top x}\in P(A,b).$$

A conformal circuit decomposition of $p-v_0$ contains a circuit with positive $t$-coordinate. Its $u$-coordinates are nonnegative and its $w$-coordinate is negative, so it admits a finite maximal improving step from $v_0$.

The construction adds only two variables and one equality. It does not assume a positive feasibility margin, nondegeneracy or full row rank.

Therefore, a uniformly strongly polynomial primitive that returns one improving circuit or a correct “none” on this family would already solve unrestricted feasibility. Applying it to the three bounded certificate systems above would solve the entire requested LP output problem with at most three calls.

That primitive has not been constructed. The reduction prevents treating direction selection as an inexpensive local operation merely because a direction, once supplied, is easy to follow.

1. Exact restricted-progress reduction

For arbitrary rational feasibility data $A,b$, construct

$$P(A,b)=
\left\{(u,t,w)\ge0:
Au-bt=0,\quad \mathbf1^\top u+t+w=1
\right\}.$$

This is a nonempty compact polytope, with the explicitly known vertex

$$v_0=(0,0,1).$$

Use the objective $-t$.

Then:

$$Ax=b,\ x\ge0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there is a feasible strictly improving circuit at }v_0.$$

Every such circuit $g$ gives a feasible solution directly:

$$x=\frac{g_u}{g_t}.$$

Conversely, a feasible $x$ gives the feasible lifted point

$$p=\frac{(x,1,0)}{1+\mathbf1^\top x}.$$

A conformal circuit decomposition of $p-v_0$ has a summand with positive $t$-coordinate. Its only possible negative coordinate is $w$, so its maximal augmentation from $v_0$ is finite and improving.

The construction adds two variables and one equality, preserves polynomial encoding sizes, and needs only coefficient copying, ordinary arithmetic and linear algebra.

This establishes that finding even one improving circuit from a known vertex of this compact family already contains unrestricted feasibility. It does not prove that the primitive is impossible.

2. Full certificates need at most three calls to that missing primitive

The primitive need only return an actual improving circuit or a correct Boolean “none.” A dual certificate on “none” is unnecessary because another feasibility call constructs it.

- Test $Ax=b,\ x\ge0$.

- If infeasible, solve the guaranteed-feasible Farkas system
$$A^\top(z^+-z^-)-s=0,\qquad
b^\top(z^+-z^-)=-1,\qquad z^\pm,s\ge0.$$
Return $z=z^+-z^-$. Two calls total.

- If primal feasible, test
$$Ar=0,\qquad c^\top r=-1,\qquad r\ge0.$$
If feasible, return the original feasible point and $r$. Two calls total.

- Otherwise solve the guaranteed-feasible linear optimal-pair system
$$Ax=b,\quad A^\top(y^+-y^-)+s=c,\quad
c^\top x-b^\top(y^+-y^-)=0,$$
with $x,y^\pm,s\ge0$. Three calls total.

All systems have $O(m+n)$ rows and columns and polynomial input encoding growth. This is a paid full-output reduction using classical alternatives and duality, not an acquired LP algorithm.
